questions.q: A producer uses `acks=1`. The leader writes the record and answers, then its broker fails before either follower copies the record. What happens to the record?

options.t: It is lost, even though the producer was told it succeeded
A follower recovers it from the producer's buffer
options.why: Followers copy from the leader, never from the producer.

options.t: The producer retries automatically and it is never lost
options.why: The producer already had its acknowledgement, so it has nothing to retry.

options.t: It stays readable on the failed broker's disk for consumers
options.why: Consumers read from the new leader, which never had it.

questions.explain: With `acks=1` the leader answers after writing its own log, without waiting for followers, so a record is lost if the leader fails before they copy it.

questions.q: What does `acks=0` mean for the producer?

options.t: The leader waits for zero followers but still sends the producer an answer
options.why: That is acks=1.

options.t: It doesn't wait for any answer, so it never learns if the write worked
The producer sends to zero partitions until metadata loads
options.why: acks has nothing to do with partition choice.

options.t: The record is written to all replicas before sending
options.why: Producers don't write to replicas; acks=0 waits for nothing.

questions.explain: With `acks=0` the producer doesn't wait: the record counts as sent once in the socket buffer, retries have no effect, and the returned offset is always -1.

questions.q: A topic has `min.insync.replicas=2`. Its ISR shrinks to the leader alone. A producer with `acks=1` sends a record. What happens?

options.t: It is refused with NotEnoughReplicasException
options.why: That refusal applies only to acks=all writes.

options.t: It waits until a second replica rejoins
options.why: acks=1 waits only for the leader.

options.t: The producer upgrades itself to acks=all
options.why: Producers don't change acks by themselves.

options.t: It succeeds: min.insync.replicas only applies to acks=all

questions.explain: `min.insync.replicas` takes effect with `acks=all`; with `acks=1` or `0` it refuses nothing.

questions.q: A topic has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`. Two brokers holding its followers go down. A producer with `acks=all` sends a record. What does it get?

options.t: A success, with one copy
options.why: With acks=all, the ISR (1) is below the minimum (2), so the write is refused.

options.t: An error such as NotEnoughReplicasException, so it knows the write wasn't stored safely
A success after the followers come back, however long that takes
options.why: The write is refused, not held.

options.t: A silent drop with no error
options.why: The producer is told the write failed.

questions.explain: With `acks=all`, a write is refused when the ISR is smaller than `min.insync.replicas`, and the producer gets an exception. Kafka prefers refusing to accepting a write with too few copies.

questions.q: Can a consumer read from a follower replica instead of the leader?

options.t: No; all reads and writes must go to the partition leader
options.why: All writes go to the leader, but reads can go to followers.

options.t: Only if unclean leader election is enabled
options.why: Follower reads are unrelated to unclean election.

options.t: Yes, for example a follower in the consumer's own rack
Only for compacted topics
options.why: Cleanup policy doesn't decide where reads go.

questions.explain: All writes go to the leader; reads can go to the leader or followers. `client.rack` tells the cluster which rack the consumer is in, matched with the brokers' `broker.rack`.

questions.q: A topic has `message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime`. What timestamp do its records carry?

options.t: The time the broker appended the record
The time the producer created the record
options.why: That is CreateTime, the default.

options.t: The time a consumer first read it
options.why: Reading never changes a record.

options.t: No timestamp at all
options.why: Every record has a timestamp; this setting chooses whose.

questions.explain: `message.timestamp.type` is `CreateTime` (the producer's time, the default) or `LogAppendTime` (the broker's).

questions.q: A producer sends a 3 MiB record to a topic with default settings, also with default producer settings. What happens?

options.t: The broker splits it into three 1 MiB records
options.why: Kafka never splits records.

options.t: It is written, because only batches have a size limit
options.why: A single 3 MiB record exceeds the producer's own request size limit.

options.t: It is compressed until it fits
options.why: Compression is off by default and wouldn't be applied to fit a limit.

options.t: It fails with RecordTooLargeException, a non-retriable error, because it exceeds the 1 MiB defaults

questions.explain: The producer's `max.request.size` defaults to 1 MiB and the broker's `message.max.bytes` / topic `max.message.bytes` to about 1 MiB, so the send fails with `RecordTooLargeException`, which retrying won't fix.

questions.q: A consumer uses auto-commit and hands each polled record to a background thread pool, then polls again at once. When can records be missed (never processed)?

options.t: Never: auto-commit always gives at-least-once delivery, whatever the threading
options.why: Only if every record from a poll is processed before the next poll.

options.t: After an auto-commit covers records the pool hasn't processed, then a crash
Only when the topic is compacted
options.why: The risk comes from committing ahead of processing, whatever the topic.

options.t: Only when acks=0 is used by the producer
options.why: This is about the consumer's commits, not producer acks.

questions.explain: Auto-commit gives at-least-once only if all records from a `poll` are processed before the next `poll` or close. Hand-off to other threads lets the committed offset get ahead of processing.

questions.q: With the classic group protocol in Kafka 4.3, what is the default `partition.assignment.strategy`?

options.t: [RoundRobinAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]
options.why: Round robin is available, but the default list starts with RangeAssignor, which is the one used.

options.t: [StickyAssignor]
options.why: Sticky is available but not the default.

options.t: [RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]
[uniform, range]
options.why: Those are the broker's server-side assignors for the consumer protocol.

questions.explain: The default is `[RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]`: Range is used, and having CooperativeSticky in the list allows upgrading with a single rolling bounce that removes Range.

questions.q: With the classic group protocol, which statements about `heartbeat.interval.ms` and `session.timeout.ms` are right?

options.t: A consumer that stops heartbeating for session.timeout.ms (45 s by default) is considered dead
The heartbeat interval should be higher than the session timeout
options.why: It must be lower, typically no more than a third.

options.t: heartbeat.interval.ms is typically set to no more than one third of the session timeout
Heartbeats are sent only from inside poll()
options.why: Heartbeating and polling are separate; that is why max.poll.interval.ms exists.

options.t: These settings also apply under group.protocol=consumer
options.why: Under the consumer protocol they are set on the broker and can't be used on the client.

questions.explain: Classic protocol: the session timeout (default 45 s) detects failures by missing heartbeats, and the heartbeat interval (default 3 s) must be lower, typically one third or less.

questions.q: A consumer reads a topic written by a transactional producer. Which isolation level hides records from aborted transactions?

options.t: read_uncommitted, the default
options.why: The default returns aborted transactional records too.

options.t: serializable
options.why: Kafka has no such isolation level.

options.t: read_latest
options.why: Kafka has no such isolation level.

options.t: read_committed: it returns only committed transactional records, up to the last stable offset

questions.explain: `isolation.level=read_committed` returns only committed transactional records, and only up to the last stable offset; non-transactional records are always returned.

questions.q: A developer tries transactions on a single-broker development cluster with default broker settings, and transactional producers fail to initialise. What is the likely cause?

options.t: The transaction state topic needs 3 brokers by default
Transactions need ZooKeeper
options.why: 4.x has no ZooKeeper; transactions run in KRaft clusters.

options.t: Transactions need acks=1
options.why: Transactions need idempotence, which needs acks=all.

options.t: Transactions only work on compacted topics, and the default policy is delete
options.why: Transactions work with any topic.

questions.explain: `transaction.state.log.replication.factor` defaults to 3 (min ISR 2), so by default transactions need at least three brokers; a single-broker dev setup lowers these settings.

questions.q: Which statement about KRaft combined mode (`process.roles=broker,controller`) is right?

options.t: It is required in production
options.why: The docs recommend against it in critical deployments.

options.t: Simple for development, not recommended for critical deployments
It is the only mode Kafka 4.x supports, since ZooKeeper was removed
options.why: Separate broker and controller roles are supported, and recommended for production.

options.t: It removes the need to format storage
options.why: Every server must be formatted, combined or not.

questions.explain: Combined servers are simpler for small setups, but controllers can't then be rolled or scaled separately; the docs don't recommend them in critical deployments.

questions.q: A new Kafka 4.3 server won't start because its log directory is blank. What must be done first?

options.t: Nothing; Kafka 4.3 formats a blank log directory automatically on first start
options.why: 4.x no longer formats blank storage automatically.

options.t: Start ZooKeeper
options.why: 4.x has no ZooKeeper.

options.t: Generate a cluster ID and format the storage with kafka-storage
Create the __consumer_offsets topic by hand
options.why: Internal topics are created by the cluster.

questions.explain: Each server is formatted with a cluster ID (`kafka-storage random-uuid`, then `kafka-storage format`). Kafka no longer auto-formats blank storage, because that could hide an error.

questions.q: A developer runs `kafka-console-consumer --topic orders --from-beginning` (no `--group`) twice. What happens on the second run?

options.t: It replays the whole topic, in a new random group
It continues from the offset the first run reached before it was stopped
options.why: That needs --group, so the first run committed offsets.

options.t: It reads nothing, because the offsets were committed
options.why: Without a group, nothing was committed.

options.t: It fails because the group already exists
options.why: Each run gets a new random group.

questions.explain: Without `--group`, the console consumer uses a new `console-consumer-<n>` group with auto-commit off, so `--from-beginning` replays everything each run. With `--group`, a second run resumes.

questions.q: How can a tombstone (a keyed record with a null value) be sent with the 4.3 console producer?

options.t: Type the key followed by an empty line
options.why: An empty string is a value, not null.

options.t: Use parse.key=true with a null.marker as the value
The console producer can't send null values
options.why: It can, with null.marker.

options.t: Use the --delete-key option followed by the key to delete
options.why: There is no such option.

questions.explain: With `parse.key=true`, a `key.separator` and a `null.marker`, a field equal to the marker becomes null, which is how to send a tombstone.

questions.q: Which tool prints a topic's end offset for each partition?

options.t: kafka-get-offsets --topic <name>
kafka-storage info
options.why: That inspects a node's storage formatting, not topic offsets.

options.t: kafka-metadata-quorum describe
options.why: That describes the controller quorum.

options.t: kafka-acls --list
options.why: That lists ACLs.

questions.explain: `kafka-get-offsets --topic` prints the end offset of each partition.

questions.q: Which statement about Kafka's availability during a network partition between brokers is consistent with the Apache Kafka design documentation?

options.t: Kafka stays fully available for writes on both sides
options.why: The docs say it may not remain available during network partitions.

options.t: Kafka guarantees no unavailability at all
options.why: There is a short fail-over even for a broker failure.

options.t: It switches to eventual consistency on both sides and merges the two logs afterwards
options.why: Kafka doesn't merge divergent logs.

options.t: It stays available after a short fail-over, but may not during network partitions

questions.explain: The guarantee is that a committed message isn't lost while one in-sync replica lives; Kafka stays available after a short fail-over, but may not remain available during network partitions.

questions.q: In Kafka 4.x, the controller tracks Eligible Leader Replicas (ELR). What are they?

options.t: Replicas outside the ISR that are still safe to elect without data loss
Replicas that may be elected only if unclean election is on
options.why: ELR members are safe choices, unlike unclean election.

options.t: Controllers that can become the active controller
options.why: That is the controller quorum, not partition replicas.

options.t: Followers that serve consumer reads
options.why: Follower reads are a separate feature.

questions.explain: ELR (KIP-966) lets the controller track replicas outside the ISR that are still safe leaders; election tries an ISR member first, then an unfenced ELR member.

questions.q: Which statements about a consumer's position and its committed offset are right?

options.t: The position is the offset of the next record poll will return, and it advances with every poll
The position and committed offset are always equal
options.why: They differ until the consumer commits.

options.t: The committed offset is where a restarted consumer resumes
The committed offset is stored on the consumer's disk
options.why: Kafka stores it, so any member of the group can recover it.

options.t: The position can never move backwards
options.why: seek can rewind it.

questions.explain: There are two positions per partition: the position (next record `poll` returns, advancing on every poll) and the committed position, the last offset stored securely, which a restarted consumer recovers.

questions.q: Which limits does a topic's partition count set?

options.t: The maximum number of consumers in one group that can read it in parallel
The maximum number of consumer groups that can read it
options.why: Any number of groups can read a topic.

options.t: How many servers can share its load, since each partition must fit on one server
The maximum retention of the topic
options.why: Retention is a separate setting.

options.t: The number of producers allowed to write to it
options.why: Any number of producers can write to a topic.

questions.explain: Each partition must fit on one server, so the count caps how many servers share a topic's load, and it caps the parallelism of consumers in a group.

questions.q: A service rebuilds its cache by reading a compacted topic from offset 0. The read takes 3 days, but `delete.retention.ms` is 1 day. What risk does that create?

options.t: Some offsets will be renumbered during the read
options.why: Offsets never change.

options.t: Records will be read out of order
options.why: Compaction never reorders records.

options.t: A deleted key may survive in the rebuilt cache
The topic will switch to delete policy
options.why: The cleanup policy doesn't change by itself.

questions.explain: A reader from the start sees tombstones only if it reaches them within `delete.retention.ms`; that setting also bounds how long a full re-read may take.

questions.q: Why are topic names limited to 249 characters?

options.t: Because the producer's request header has a fixed size
options.why: The limit comes from how partitions are stored on disk.

options.t: Because each partition is a folder named <topic>-<partition> in the log directory
Because KRaft stores names in a fixed-width column
options.why: The docs give the folder naming as the reason.

options.t: There is no limit
options.why: There is a 249-character limit.

questions.explain: Each partition is a directory named after the topic and partition number, so topic names are limited to 249 characters.
